track.title: Orbiter
track.album: The Great Divide: The Last Of The Bugs

explanation.overall:
The sharpest thing about this song is its last sentence: it never finishes. "If I'm gonna lose you either way" arrives four times in the outro and never once gets its second half — no *then I'll stay*, no *then let me go*. It's a conditional with the consequence surgically removed. That's the whole idea of the title rendered as grammar: an orbiter is the one object that neither lands nor escapes, and a sentence that can't reach its own ending is exactly that shape. The measured tempo makes it worse in the best way — at 85 BPM those four repeats sit roughly 11 seconds apart, about four bars each, so the line doesn't repeat so much as come back around on a fixed period. You wait through the same amount of empty space every time, and every time it returns unresolved.

The recording backs this up rather than fighting it. In the 30-second clip, energy spikes to full scale about two seconds in, then collapses — a measured drop from 0.47 to 0.17 at the 5.7-second mark, bottoming out near 0.05, near-nothing, for a couple of seconds. So the loudest thing in that stretch is a voice with almost nothing underneath it. Then it rebuilds in three swells, each smaller than the one before: 0.84, then 0.74, then 0.56, with dips between them. That's a decaying oscillation — a circle losing altitude a little each pass. The upper two-thirds of the clip also sit brighter than the first third (spectral centroid, roughly a measure of how much treble air is in the sound, rises from about 1243 Hz to around 1440), so the swells come back thinner and higher rather than heavier. Nothing accumulates. It's slow (85 BPM, sparse — under two note-attacks per beat), minor-leaning (the key read is C# minor, though that's a chroma-based guess at 0.57 confidence, so hold it loosely).

This is a lyric-first song, and its central move is that the verbs never make contact. He stares, sings, circles, howls — every action travels outward and lands on nothing. Not one of them is *touch*, *hold*, or *have*. Even the metaphor is engineered for that: an astronaut orbiting the moon is as close as a person can get to the moon without ever reaching it.

moments.what_happens: Energy falls from 0.47 to 0.17 at 5.7 seconds and keeps sinking to about 0.05 — near-silence — after having hit full scale (1.0) around the two-second mark.
moments.why_it_hits: The arrangement goes from everything to almost nothing in under four seconds, which leaves the voice exposed with no cushion. You stop hearing a production and start hearing a person alone in a room, which is the emotional position the whole song describes.

moments.what_happens: Energy peaks at 0.84, dips to 0.40, peaks again at 0.74, dips to 0.29, peaks at 0.56 — three surges roughly four seconds apart, each one measurably weaker than the last, and each brighter (more treble) than the clip's opening third.
moments.why_it_hits: Most songs build; this one circles and loses a little every lap. Your ear expects each swell to top the one before, and it doesn't — so the arrangement itself feels like something orbiting and slowly falling, thinning out instead of arriving.

moments.what_happens: The chorus rhymes hard while it's naming real places — Watertown, ground, down all chime on the same sound — and then the astronaut and moon lines land with no rhyme at all.
moments.why_it_hits: The earthbound words are locked together by sound; the moment he leaves earth, the sonic tether snaps. You feel him float off before you consciously register the image, because the pattern that was holding the lines together simply stops.

moments.what_happens: Earlier, quoting her, wolves are people who "howl for the sound of it" — noise with no object. In the outro he takes the same animal for himself, an aging one who lost the taste for blood, and howls *for you*.
moments.why_it_hits: One word gets its meaning flipped by who's saying it. Her version was a shrug about fame; his version gives the same sound a direction and a target. It's the difference between making noise and calling to someone, and the song gets there without explaining itself once.

moments.what_happens: The song's final words are the same incomplete if-clause four times, spaced about eleven seconds apart — roughly four bars at the measured 85 BPM — with the consequence clause never supplied.
moments.why_it_hits: Your brain physically waits for the back half of that sentence, four separate times, and never gets it. The unresolved grammar does what the arrangement can't say: he isn't deciding, he's still going around. The song doesn't end so much as keep circling out of earshot.

explanation.lyric_read:
The writing splits the speaking parts with real discipline. She gets the aphorisms — the insect on a window, the crowd deciding who's beautiful, even God supposedly warning him off — all delivered as quoted speech, which lets the song's wisdom arrive secondhand instead of from a narrator lecturing you. He only gets small physical verbs in return: he clings to his seat, clutches cloth, bites his tongue. She talks; he holds on. That imbalance is the relationship in miniature.

The turn happens when the machinery that's humiliating him becomes how he sees her — a camera flash, the same red-carpet apparatus that made him bitter-drunk and losing, is the light he catches her in, and the very next admission is that this is hard *but* he feels less far. That's the song's only forward motion, and it's measured in distance closed, not distance eliminated. And note what's absent: the second verse abandons rhyme almost entirely (the leaking ceiling and the ballroom don't chime), so the section where God is supposedly telling him to leave sounds structurally unsupported — nothing rhyming to hold it up. The chorus, by contrast, snaps back into a tight rhyme on the hometown words. He's most stable when he's naming where he's from, least stable when someone's arguing he doesn't belong.
explanation.headline: It never finishes its last sentence, because an orbit never arrives.

suggestions.title: Fourth of July
suggestions.why: Same ending strategy: the outro is one short line repeated far past the point of new information while the arrangement thins out, so accumulation — not resolution — has to carry the close.

suggestions.title: Moon Song
suggestions.why: Builds an entire relationship from one held celestial image plus verbs that only travel one direction, so devotion is measured as a fixed distance that never closes into contact.

suggestions.title: All Too Well (10 Minute Version)
suggestions.why: Plants an image early inside someone else's context and hands it back at the end owned by the narrator with its meaning inverted — the same trick this song runs on the wolf and the howl.
